title: Subjunctive or indicative?
why: Once the subjunctive is formed, the learner learns to choose between the two moods: an opinion stated or denied, feelings, and cuando for habits or for the future. English uses the same verb form in all these cases, so this is where English speakers slip most (especially cuando + future), hence a lesson packed with choice exercises before the debate in the next lesson.

{"lessons": ["

To believe or not to believe

When you state something you consider true, you use the indicative (the normal verb forms). When you deny it or doubt it, Spanish switches to the subjunctive. English doesn't change the verb at all (“I think he's right” / “I don't think he's right”), so you have to train yourself to spot the switch.

Stating → indicativeDenying, doubting → subjunctive
Creo que tiene razón.No creo que tenga razón.
Pienso que es una buena idea.No pienso que sea una buena idea.
Me parece que va a llover.No me parece que vaya a llover.
Es verdad que Madrid es cara.No es verdad que Madrid sea tan cara.
Estoy seguro de que viene.No estoy seguro de que venga.

Other expressions followed by the indicative: está claro que, es evidente que, es cierto que, sé que. In the negative, they switch to the subjunctive: no está claro que, no es cierto que.

The reflex to build: look for the no before the opinion verb. Creo que → indicative; no creo que → subjunctive. With the indicative, you can use any tense: Creo que vendrá, Creo que vino ayer.

", "

Feelings: always the subjunctive

When you express a feeling or reaction (joy, annoyance, regret) to what someone else does, Spanish uses the subjunctive, even if the fact is completely real. English just says “I'm glad you're here” with a normal verb, so watch out.

ExpressionExampleEnglish
me alegro de queMe alegro de que estés aquí.I'm glad you're here.
me molesta queMe molesta que los vecinos hagan ruido.It bothers me that the neighbors make noise.
me preocupa queMe preocupa que Pablo trabaje tanto.It worries me that Pablo works so much.
me encanta queMe encanta que vengáis a vernos.I love it when you all come to see us.
es una pena queEs una pena que no puedas venir.It's a shame you can't come.
¡qué pena que…!¡Qué pena que te vayas!What a shame you're leaving!

Don't forget the de: me alegro de que (alegrarse de). And if the subject doesn't change, keep the infinitive: Me alegro de verte (I'm glad to see you), Es una pena no poder ir.

Molestar, preocupar and encantar work like gustar: me molesta, te preocupa, nos encanta.

", "

Cuando: habit or future?

After cuando, the mood depends on the time you're talking about:

You're talking about…MoodExample
a habitpresent indicativeCuando llego a casa, me ducho.
(When I get home, I take a shower.)
the pastpast indicativeCuando era pequeña, iba a la playa.
Cuando llegué, ya no había nadie.
the futurepresent subjunctiveCuando llegues, llámame.
(When you arrive, call me.)

The English speaker's trap: in “when you arrive,” English uses the plain present, so you'll be tempted to use the present indicative after cuando (“cuando llegas”). But that means a habit (“whenever you arrive”). For a future event, Spanish needs the present subjunctive: cuando llegues. And never the future (“cuando llegarás”). The future is fine in the other half of the sentence: Cuando tenga tiempo, te llamaré.

Don't confuse it with the question ¿cuándo? (with an accent), which takes the indicative or the future normally: ¿Cuándo vienes?, ¿Cuándo terminarás?

Cuando sea mayor, viviré en el campo.When I grow up, I'll live in the country.
¿Me avisas cuando termines la reunión?Will you let me know when you finish the meeting?

Summary

  • Opinion stated (creo que, es verdad que) → indicative.
  • Opinion denied (no creo que, no es verdad que) → subjunctive.
  • Feeling (me alegro de que, es una pena que) → subjunctive.
  • Cuando + habit or past → indicative; cuando + future → subjunctive.
